How to read the evidence

Implemented means the control is present in source. PASS (local) means a recorded check passed in an isolated local environment. PARTIAL means the control covers only some paths. GAP means a missing or failing control was identified. PENDING means the result needs a deployed environment or information from the group. A passing regression suite is not proof that every security requirement is satisfied.

The template’s requested sections are retained. Its Mongoose, production URL, and screenshot prompts are treated as reporting requirements, not evidence that those features already exist. Figures 1–3 are real browser captures; Figures 4–6 and 10 are visual presentations of recorded test/query output. Figures 7–9 remain explicitly pending.

1. Project Overview

Item

Group Response

Project Title

WearAware: PPE Compliance Monitoring and Worker Portal

Problem/Need Addressed

Manual PPE checks and scattered records make it difficult to review violations, monitor station activity, and give workers visibility into their own compliance history.

Target Users

Administrators manage accounts, workers, and stations; inspectors perform checkpoint duties; linked worker accounts view their own records. Visitors can view the public information pages.

Main Purpose

Record PPE inspection outcomes and present compliance information to the appropriate users, supporting workplace safety monitoring and follow-up.

Major Features

Role-based login; worker and station management; QR-based worker identification; PPE detection service integration; violation records and notifications; admin and inspector dashboards; read-only worker profile, history, QR code, and personal compliance rate.

2. MERN Architecture

React communicates with the Express API through fetch requests. Express runs on Node.js and calls repository.js, which uses the native MongoDB driver for queries, aggregation joins, indexes, and transactions. This is a MongoDB–Express–React–Node stack, but it does not implement the template’s requested Mongoose ODM layer. If Mongoose is mandatory, this remains an assignment requirement to address. [S1–S5]

Architecture A. Current local implementation and supporting integrations.

Component

Technology Used

Role in Our Project

Frontend

Marketing pages, role dashboards, forms, transitions, and API requests.

Backend

Node.js / Express 5

HTTP routes, authentication, role checks, validation, and business logic.

Data-access layer

MongoDB native driver 6; no ODM

Repository functions and application-level reference checks; no Mongoose models.

Database

MongoDB replica set

Persistent collections, indexes, and transactional relationship cleanup.

API communication

2.1 Request-Response Flow

Example: a worker opens “My overview” after signing in. The compliance percentage uses all of that worker’s recorded scans, not only the current history page.

Step

What Happens in Our Application

1. React/UI Event

UserDashboard loads the personal overview and reads the login token from localStorage.

2. HTTP Request

GET /api/user/dashboard?page=1 with Authorization: Bearer <token>.

3. Express Route

/api/user router applies requireAuth and requireRole('user') before its dashboard handler.

4. Controller/Logic

Validate page; reload the authenticated account; resolve worker_id from MongoDB. Client-supplied worker/user IDs do not determine ownership.

5. MongoDB Operation

Find the linked worker; aggregate compliant/violation totals; match detections by worker_id; sort, skip, and limit history to 20; join station labels.

6. API Response

JSON includes account, worker profile, stats, history, page, pageSize, and totalPages. An unlinked account receives HTTP 409.

7. UI Update

Display profile, station, history, and compliance = compliant ÷ total × 100, rounded to one decimal. With no scans, show “No scans yet” rather than 100%.

4. Security Analysis of Our Project

This review identifies concrete implementation risks. Planned controls below are recommendations for the next revision, not changes completed during document preparation.

Area

Potential Risk in Our Project

Impact

Planned Control

Authentication

JWT lives in localStorage; recovery responses distinguish nonexistent and pending accounts. No login throttle is configured.

Token theft after XSS; account enumeration; repeated guessing.

Add throttling and uniform recovery responses; review session storage and expiration policy.

Authorization / RBAC

Worker portal ownership is enforced, but general worker/device GET routes allow broad inspector access; scan creation lacks a station-ownership check.

Inspectors may access unrelated worker data or submit mismatched scan associations.

Scope all inspector reads and writes to assigned stations and validate worker–station–inspector relationships.

Input validation

Repository rejects object-valued query fields and invalid IDs, but server-side format/length checks are inconsistent and mostly hand-written.

Malformed data, misleading 500 errors, and reliance on browser validation.

Define server-side request schemas, allowed fields, field lengths, and consistent 400 responses.

Database

Local startup binds loopback but does not configure MongoDB authorization or TLS. Production DB permissions are unverified.

An exposed or overprivileged DB could reveal or alter worker records.

Use a dedicated application DB identity, restricted network access, TLS, backup/restore tests, and retention rules.

API

No rate limiter or security-header middleware found. Malformed JSON returned an HTML stack in a local probe.

Resource abuse and disclosure of internal paths/implementation details.

Centralize safe errors; cap requests; configure appropriate response headers; disable framework disclosure.

Passwords

users.password_hash is bcrypt-hashed, but reset handling also stores and returns temp_password in plaintext.

Compromise of reset records can reveal usable passwords.

Replace temporary passwords with expiring single-use reset tokens; remove plaintext reset credentials and invalidate affected secrets.

Deployment

Frontend/API/inference URLs and CORS are localhost-specific. No live HTTPS URLs were provided.

Broken production requests or unencrypted transport if deployed unchanged.

Environment-based endpoints; HTTPS API/frontend/inference; controlled CORS; authenticated WSS.

Other: live alerts

WebSocket server has no connection authentication shown and sends violations to every open client.

Worker names, IDs, and violation details may reach unauthorized recipients.

Authenticate connections, enforce per-inspector subscriptions, and minimize alert payloads.

Priority before public deployment: fix credential recovery, WebSocket access, inspector scope, and safe error handling; then verify TLS, database access, validation, and request limits. The 16 passing regression tests cover selected behaviors and do not remove these findings. [S3–S9, S11]

5. Authentication and Authorization

POST /api/auth/login looks up the submitted email, checks that the account is active, compares the password with bcrypt, and signs an 8-hour JWT. Protected requests verify the signature, reload the account, reject deactivated users, and check whether updated_at makes the token stale. The current database role replaces the token’s role claim, so an old claim cannot restore admin access. [S3, S4]

React uses the returned role to select a dashboard. Server middleware remains the enforcement point. A “user” account must link to a real worker, and a unique partial index prevents two accounts from claiming the same worker. The worker portal derives ownership from the current account, not a request parameter. [S5–S7]

Description

Allowed Functions

Restricted Functions

admin

System administrator

Manage users, workers, stations, assignments, activity, reset requests, and organization reports.

Inspector-only scan and override APIs and user-only dashboard are not granted automatically.

inspector

Record detections; review inspector history; handle own alerts; update own profile and assigned-station workflows.

User administration and admin reports. General worker/device reads remain too broad and are documented as a gap.

View own profile, station, scan history, all-time compliance, and employee-ID QR code.

Admin/inspector APIs; record mutation; other workers’ history.

Guest

Protected database resources and dashboards.

7. Database Design and Security

MongoDB stores the application records. The project keeps integer business IDs from its earlier database design, while MongoDB also maintains internal _id values. Relationships use integer references and $lookup aggregation joins rather than Mongoose populate. PPE lists are embedded arrays. [S5]

Collection

Purpose / Important Fields

Embedded / Referenced

Security Consideration

roles

Account permissions: id, name.

users.role_id → roles.id.

Unique role names; account management is admin-only.

users

Login/account: id, role_id, worker_id, email, full_name, password_hash, is_active, updated_at.

References roles and optionally one worker.

Unique email and partial unique worker_id; use limited response projections; never return password hashes.

devices

Checkpoint/station: id, device_id, label, location, inspector_id, required_ppe, is_active.

References inspector user; embeds required_ppe array.

Restrict management; scope inspector reads and scan submissions more tightly.

workers

Worker registry: id, employee_id, full_name, position, contact_number, device_id, status.

References station; referenced by accounts and detections.

Unique employee ID; protect identity and contact data; preserve ownership constraints.

detections

Scan result: id, worker_id, device_id, inspector_id, result, detected_ppe, missing_ppe, confidence_score, photo_url, detected_at.

References worker, station, inspector; embeds PPE arrays.

Filter by owner/role; minimize photos and identifiers; define retention and access policy.

notifications

Violation alerts: id, detection_id, inspector_id, is_read, created_at.

References detection and inspector.

HTTP notification routes scope to inspector; separate WebSocket path still needs authorization.

password_reset_requests

Recovery queue: id, email, reason, status, temp_password, created_at.

Email-based association; no repository foreign-key relationship.

Plaintext temp_password is an unresolved gap. Use expiring reset tokens instead.

_counters / _migration

Internal ID allocation and migration state.

Atomic counters; postgres-v1 migration marker.

Internal operational data; no public editing interface; protect migration credentials and backups.

Integrity and operational controls

ensureIndexes creates unique record IDs, unique role/email/device/employee identifiers, and the partial unique worker-account link. Repository checks reject unknown referenced records. Selected deletion operations run in transactions: deleting a worker clears linked account and detection worker IDs while preserving historical scans. Tests confirm that a newly unlinked worker account is blocked with HTTP 409.

Startup requires a completed postgres-v1 migration marker before it starts the API. A new empty database therefore needs an explicit migration/initialization plan. The local launcher creates a replica set bound to 127.0.0.1; it does not configure authorization or TLS. Production access controls and restore procedures remain pending. Compass is an administrative viewer/editor for this database, not its hosting or application runtime.

8.1 Deployment Architecture

Architecture B. Proposed target only; no hosting provider or live URL is claimed.

Deployment sequence and acceptance

First resolve the high-priority security gaps in Section 4. Then provision a restricted MongoDB replica set, migrate/initialize and verify records plus indexes, configure API secrets and allowed origins, deploy the API and inference service, and build the frontend against their HTTPS URLs. Finally verify all three roles, CRUD, owned history, camera access, WSS delivery, backups/restoration, safe errors, and throttling against the deployed environment. Repeat the Section 9 checks and replace pending evidence with actual live captures.

Reflection Questions

What changed when your application moved from local development to deployment?

A completed production move has not yet been verified, so we cannot report it as finished. Our local build depends on localhost frontend, API, inference, and WebSocket endpoints. Deployment will require configurable service URLs, trusted HTTPS/WSS, production CORS and secrets, a restricted database connection, and a verified migration/initialization process. Running Compass alone does not start the frontend or Express API.

What security weakness did your testing reveal?

A malformed JSON request produced an HTML response containing a development stack trace and filesystem path. Source review also found plaintext temporary passwords in the reset-request collection, unauthenticated WebSocket broadcasts, missing request throttling/security headers, and inspector data-scope gaps. Passing authentication tests did not prove that all access paths were safe.

How did your group address the identified weakness?

The current worker portal already applies server-derived ownership, current-database role checks, unique worker-account links, and a read-only dashboard. Automated tests verify those protections, including forged IDs and stale role claims. The newly documented error, recovery, WebSocket, and inspector-scope findings remain unresolved in the reviewed code. They are listed as required follow-up work rather than described as completed fixes.

What additional security improvement would you implement with more development time?

We would replace plaintext reset passwords with expiring single-use reset tokens, authenticate and scope WebSocket subscriptions, enforce inspector ownership on every relevant route, centralize validation and safe errors, and add throttling plus deployment-appropriate headers. We would then verify TLS, least-privilege database access, backup recovery, and the same role/data-ownership cases on the actual deployed services.

Appendix B. Safe Configuration Example

This example contains placeholders only. It is included as backend.env.example alongside the report, without restoring or changing the application’s configuration. Do not commit real credentials. Frontend URLs are currently hardcoded and require a separate code change before hosting.

# Local development example only — no real credentials.

PORT=5000

WS_PORT=8080

MONGODB_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/wearaware?replicaSet=wearaware-rs

MONGODB_DB=wearaware

JWT_SECRET=replace-with-a-long-random-secret

EMAIL_USER=

EMAIL_PASS=

# Legacy PostgreSQL settings: needed only for migration/rollback.

DB_HOST=localhost

DB_PORT=5432

DB_NAME=wearaware

DB_USER=replace-with-migration-user

DB_PASSWORD=replace-with-migration-password

Local run and verification notes

The root frontend package uses npm run dev; it has no npm start script. The backend uses npm --prefix src/wearawarebackend start. The local database helper is npm --prefix src/wearawarebackend run db:local. Start only the components needed for the intended environment, and ensure the required database migration state and secrets are configured. Compass is optional for viewing data and is not the process that runs the application.

To repeat the existing regression suite: npm --prefix src/wearawarebackend test. It creates temporary replica-set databases; it does not test the production database. The supplemental JSON file records actual isolated observations from this report preparation. Synthetic fixtures are intentionally separate from real worker data.
